guides.title: Your skin barrier
guides.subtitle: A starting point for understanding everyday skin comfort.
sections: The outer skin layer helps limit water loss and acts as a boundary between the body and its environment. Skin comfort is influenced by products, weather and underlying skin conditions.
Think of the surface as an organised layer rather than an empty canvas. Changes in dryness, stinging or redness can have several causes; a picture alone cannot identify the cause.
A consultation may explore cleansing habits, moisturisers, sun exposure and the timing of symptoms. Persistent irritation may need medical assessment before a cosmetic treatment is considered.
Write down products used, when symptoms started and any previous reactions. Introduce this history at your appointment rather than relying on a skin-type label.
Could this be irritation or an underlying skin condition? Which products should I discuss? Should an elective procedure wait until my skin is settled?
This sheet explains a concept, not a treatment routine. Seek medical advice for persistent or worsening symptoms.
guides.caption: Natural cheek texture in close-up.

guides.title: Pigmentation explained
guides.subtitle: Similar-looking marks can have different causes.
sections: Pigmentation describes differences in skin colour. A dark area can relate to several processes, so a single label such as dark spot is not a diagnosis.
Colour, distribution, onset and previous inflammation all help a clinician build a history. Similar appearances may require different approaches, especially across different skin tones.
The clinic lists a Signature Pigmentation Programme, peels and other skin treatments. A clinician first needs to identify the type of mark and decide whether a cosmetic treatment is appropriate.
Bring a timeline, relevant medicines and details of earlier peels, lasers or reactions. Ask whether the mark needs diagnostic assessment before any cosmetic treatment.
What type of pigmentation do you suspect? What are the alternatives? How could treatment affect my skin tone? What happens if pigment returns?
New or changing individual lesions need assessment. No treatment can promise permanently even skin. Irritation and procedures can themselves lead to colour changes.
guides.caption: Flat areas of uneven pigmentation on the cheek.

guides.title: Skin analysis
guides.subtitle: A conversation supported by imaging, not replaced by it.
sections: Skin analysis combines discussion and examination; some pathways also use photographs or imaging tools to document visible concerns.
A scan can help organise a conversation about texture, tone or appearance. Lighting, image quality and the tool used affect what is shown.
Harley Street Aesthetics offers a free photo-based skin analysis. It can help organise questions about visible concerns, but a clinician must confirm the concern and any treatment plan.
Check how photographs are stored and used. Describe symptoms and history even when they do not show clearly in an image.
Who reviews the result? What can this tool assess reliably? Can I decline photography? Does the result change the options we discuss?
Automated analysis cannot rule out skin cancer or explain every skin change. Do not use a reassuring score to postpone medical assessment of a concerning lesion.
guides.caption: A clinician examining facial skin under magnification.

guides.title: Sun protection
guides.subtitle: Protection is a combination of habits and products.
sections: Sun protection aims to reduce exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Shade, protective clothing and sunscreen work together.
SPF and UVA protection describe different aspects of a sunscreen. Neither number means you can remain in the sun indefinitely.
The NHS advises sunscreen of at least SPF 30 with strong UVA protection, alongside shade and clothing. Follow product instructions and reapply as directed.
Check expiry dates and whether a product suits your skin. Ask your clinician about additional protection around a procedure or a medicine that increases sun sensitivity.
Does my medicine affect sun sensitivity? When can I use sunscreen after my procedure? What protection is appropriate for my usual activities?
Sunscreen does not block all UV exposure. Avoid burning and do not use tanning as a measure of skin health. Personal advice may differ after a procedure.
guides.caption: Sunscreen being spread across the forearm.

guides.title: Hydrating serums
guides.subtitle: What a humectant can do.
sections: A serum describes a product format. The word alone tells you little about the ingredients or their purpose.
Humectants, such as glycerin and hyaluronic acid, attract water. A serum may contain them alongside other ingredients.
Look at the full formula and how it feels on your skin. A simple moisturiser may already contain the same humectants.
Bring the products you use to a consultation. Two different bottles can contain overlapping ingredients.
What would this add to my routine? Does my moisturiser already meet that need?
A topical serum is different from an injectable treatment. A product that repeatedly stings or irritates deserves reassessment.
guides.caption: A topical serum and glass dropper.

guides.title: Choosing a moisturiser
guides.subtitle: A closer look at lotions, creams and ointments.
sections: Moisturisers help skin retain water. Lotions, creams and ointments differ in texture and how they feel after application.
Humectants attract water, emollients smooth the surface and occlusives help limit moisture loss. One product can combine these functions.
A lighter lotion may feel comfortable on oily areas. A richer cream or ointment may suit drier areas. Individual preferences matter.
Note which textures feel comfortable and which products cause stinging. Fragrance-free options may be helpful for sensitive skin.
Is a different texture worth trying? Which ingredients overlap with products I already use?
Persistent cracking, itch or irritation may need medical assessment. A moisturiser alone cannot explain the cause.
guides.caption: Cream moisturiser in an open pot.

guides.title: RF Needling
guides.subtitle: How fine needles deliver radiofrequency energy.
sections: RF Needling uses an array of fine needles to deliver radiofrequency energy beneath the skin surface. The energy produces local heating.
The cartridge, treatment area and device settings affect where heat is delivered. Device selection and use require a trained clinician.
The clinic lists Virtue RF Needling for concerns such as acne scars, visible pores, uneven texture and early loss of firmness. A clinician decides whether it suits your skin and goals.
Discuss skin tone, scarring history, previous procedures and medicines. Ask how the practitioner assesses suitability and manages unwanted pigmentation or burns.
Why this device? What evidence supports my indication? How many sessions are proposed? What is the recovery plan and total cost?
Serious complications reported with some uses include burns, scarring, fat loss and nerve injury. Ask about the risks for your skin and the proposed device. This is not a home treatment.
guides.caption: A representative RF handpiece and needle cartridge; device designs vary.

guides.title: Chemical peels
guides.subtitle: The formulation and assessment matter more than the name.
sections: A chemical peel uses a controlled chemical treatment to affect skin layers. Products and peel depths vary; the word peel alone does not describe their intensity.
Depth, formulation, application and individual skin response influence the effect. A cosmetic acid product and a professional peel are not interchangeable.

The clinic offers clinician-selected chemical peels, including named programmes such as VI Peel and Cosmelan. They serve different concerns and have different preparation, recovery and home-care needs.
Share previous pigment changes, sensitive skin, medicines and earlier resurfacing. Get written preparation and aftercare instructions for the actual product.
What peel and depth are you proposing? Is it suitable for my skin tone? What downtime should I allow? What happens if healing is delayed?
Peels can cause irritation, burns, colour changes and scarring. This sheet is not a recipe or a set of instructions for performing a peel at home.
guides.caption: A peel brush and preparation bowl.

guides.title: IPL & laser facials
guides.subtitle: Light-based procedures are not all the same.
sections: Harley Street lists IPL facials and carbon laser facials. IPL uses a range of light wavelengths; a laser has a different light-delivery principle.
A device’s target and the way energy interacts with tissue shape its intended use. A marketing name is not enough to compare two procedures.
The clinic lists IPL for selected redness, thread veins and sun spots, and a carbon laser facial for oiliness, visible pores and dullness. The right option depends on the concern and your skin type.
Discuss your skin tone, recent tanning, medicines and previous reactions. Ask about eye protection and whether a test area is appropriate.
What is the exact device? What is the intended target? How do you reduce burn and pigment risks? What is the alternative if I am unsuitable?

Light-based treatments can cause burns, colour changes, scarring or eye injury. IPL is not right for every skin tone or type of pigmentation; melasma needs particular care. New or changing marks need medical assessment first.
guides.caption: An IPL handpiece and protective eyewear. A laser uses a different light source.

bonuses.title: Your consultation companion
bonuses.subtitle: Turn a concern into a clearer conversation.
sections: My priorities
Write the concern in your own words. What would a useful improvement look like? What would you prefer to avoid?
My history
List previous treatments, medicines, allergies, relevant conditions and any previous reactions. Keep this personal copy private.
My questions
Ask about diagnosis, options including no treatment, expected benefit, uncertainty, downtime, risks and total costs.
My decision space
Record what you understood and what still needs explaining. You can ask for time before deciding.
My next step
Note who will contact you, any agreed investigations and when to review. An appointment is not a commitment to treatment.

bonuses.title: Compare your options
bonuses.subtitle: A printable framework for an informed choice.
sections: Option A / Option B / No treatment
For each option, note its purpose and why it is being considered. Include waiting or monitoring where appropriate.
Benefit and evidence
Write down the outcome discussed, how likely it is, how long it may last and which evidence supports it.
Risks and recovery
Record common effects, serious risks, time away from usual activities and any care responsibilities.
Time and cost
Include sessions, maintenance, follow-up, travel and any extra charges. Ask what is included in the quoted price.
My choice
What fits your priorities? What information is missing? Discuss this worksheet with the treating clinician.

bonuses.title: Your follow-up notebook
bonuses.subtitle: Keep the plan, instructions and contact details together.
sections: My agreed plan
Record the treatment or investigation, date and clinician. Use the written instructions from your own treating team.
My instructions
Attach the actual preparation and aftercare information supplied. This notebook does not replace procedure-specific instructions.
My observations
Note the date and changes you want to discuss. Ask the team which changes are expected and which require urgent contact.
My contact details
Write down the clinic’s routine contact and urgent out-of-hours plan. Do not wait for a routine review if urgent advice is needed.
My review
Record follow-up dates, questions and any agreed next step. Keep private medical details on your own device or printed copy.
